📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

In a recent development, place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; rapidly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

According to recent reports, uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

Recent findings suggest that in particular, frog fastenings are having a resurgence, bringing a fanciful finishing touch to everything from minimalist wool peacoats to tailored military-inspired jackets. Typically constructed from fabric or braided cord, the fasteners consist of a knotted button and a loop. Originally designed to secure garments, the closures have evolved into a more ornamental role with intricate shapes and floral-like designs.

Industry observers note that while they may seem new for the season, frog-fastener jackets have a history that spans centuries. In Chinese dress, knotted closures known as pankou have long appeared on garments such as the qipao and tangzhuang. By the 18th and 19th centuries, frogging had also become a feature of European military uniforms, worn by cavalry regiments whose fitted jackets were adorned with braided cords.

Fashion has revisited the detail since then. Oscar de la Renta incorporated frog fastenings into his designs in the 1990s, while Valentino explored versions for its fall 2015 couture collection. More recently, for fall 2026, designers reinterpreted knotted closures: At Kallmeyer, black toggles punctuated a gilded jacquard jacket, while Kim Shui incorporated the detail into fur-trimmed blazers and opera jackets. Meanwhile, labels like Khaite and Ann Demeulemeester embraced military-inspired looks featuring ornamental braiding and embellished fronts.

It has been revealed that today’s store-rack versions range from collarless blazers with understated knots to dramatic outerwear designs featuring detailed cording. Brands like Róhe have introduced contemporary takes on frogging, while Hong Kong–based fashion label Sau Lee has reimagined traditional Tang-style jackets with modern silhouettes.

Rather than reinventing jackets entirely, designers are proving that something as minuscule as a fastening can make a familiar silhouette feel fresh again for the season. Ahead, shop our favorite takes on the look.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

According to recent reports, what’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

A 1972 advertisement for the Pogue.

In a recent development, one of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

In a recent development, the best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison.

Caroline is the co-CEO of Alameda Research and Sam’s on/off girlfriend.

Anthony Boyle plays Sam Bankman-Fried.

Sam is the CEO of FTX, and Caroline’s on/off girlfriend.

In a recent development, since originating the role of Scorpius Malfoy in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, for which he won a freakin’ Olivier Award, Boyle has been dominating the based-on-a-true-story genre. Trabucco is the co-CEO of Alameda Research and Sam’s friend from MIT.

Ryan became the CEO of FTX Digital Markets after working at Alameda Reserch.

#42979. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📅 13 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (378 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (378 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights.
  • Sources indicate that the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home.
  • More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

Sources indicate that the seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#42977. Florence Pugh Is Fed Up With Faces Being Scrutinized Online—We All Should Be

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (611 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Florence Pugh Is Fed Up With Faces Being Scrutinized Online—We All Should Be

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it can be tough, being a celebrity.
  • Sources indicate that particularly for women, of course.
  • In a recent development, one star who has found herself at the centre of online scrutiny this week is former Vogue cover star Florence Pugh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it can be tough, being a celebrity. Hear me out! Sure, it comes with money, acclaim, and unfettered access to luxury fashion. But it also tends to mean millions of people feel entitled to vocalize their opinion on your looks, which is when things inevitably tend to get a little trickier.

Sources indicate that particularly for women, of course. And particularly when self-appointed social media detectives start scrutinizing every inch of a woman’s face, speculating about what she may or may not have had “done.” Is it a facelift or filler? A little Botox or upper blepharoplasty? It’s safe to say that no tweak, tightening or treatment—real or imagined—goes unnoticed, or increasingly, unremarked upon.

In a recent development, one star who has found herself at the centre of online scrutiny this week is former Vogue cover star Florence Pugh. In an Instagram Reel titled, “Is it just me or does Hollywood hate round faces?” a writer compared an older photograph of Pugh with a more recent one, suggesting the 30-year-old East of Eden star’s face shape had changed in the interim.

Florence Pugh at the 2026 Governors Awards.

“People are saying that Florence Pugh has fallen victim to Hollywood’s war on round faces,” the writer indicates. “Don’t get me wrong, Florence Pugh still looks beautiful, but Hollywood seems to have this thing against softer features.” The reel goes on to discuss the “sculpted” and “snatched” look that has become the beauty ideal in the entertainment world, suggesting that women are increasingly pursuing sharper jawlines as a result. The clip caught the attention of Pugh herself, who commented on the post.

Industry observers note that “Guys, I turned 30,” the actor wrote. “I’m a woman. [Bodies] and faces change. It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing. Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.”.

Florence Pugh at the 96th Annual Academy Awards in 2024.

It has been revealed that pugh’s exasperated response illustrates just how exhausting it is to be a woman in the public eye—a woman full stop—where you’re damned if you do and damned if you don’t. (Pugh sadly has previous experience with internet trolls, she memorably told online body shamers to “grow up” after they weighed in on her dress for the Valentino Haute Couture show in Rome.) On the one hand, women are celebrated for embracing the entirely normal aging process. (Take Olivia Colman and Sarah Jessica Parker, for example, who have been praised for their chic silver hair.) On the other, they risk being accused of “letting themselves go” if they don’t continue to look exactly as they did when they first entered the spotlight. And if they do choose to have a little help along the way, as is entirely their prerogative? That gets dissected ad nauseam, too.

Sources indicate that of course, celebrities shouldn’t be exempt from conversations about beauty standards, and the more we question the normalization of cosmetic procedures, the more we can make natural aging feel, well, normal. But there’s a difference between a healthy conversation about unrealistic beauty ideals and picking apart an individual woman’s appearance.

Speculating about what someone has or hasn’t had done is just as damaging as criticizing lines, wrinkles, or any other natural signs of aging. Both reinforce the idea that a woman’s face is fair game. What we’re really doing? Perpetuating the same impossible beauty standards that hurt us all in the long run.

In a recent development, “Throughout the process, I was thinking of Katniss and President Snow and her courage in leading a rebellion against the Capitol and Snow,” Noah says, adding that she had written the track in under an hour. Luckily, Noah gave Cosmo the first look at her new music video for “Ash and Snow.” Come for the achingly beautiful visuals, and stay for the vengeance, justice, and sacrifice that shaped the song.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same company behind A Ma Maniére.
  • Social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Menswear guys love Japanese denim. Menswear guys also love sneakers. So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge? That seems to be the thinking behind the newly introduced Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko.’.

Social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same company behind A Ma Maniére. Over the years, it’s worked with Nike on everything from milk-inspired Dunks to Air Pennys. The shop’s last proper Jordan collab was an extremely hairy Air Jordan 6 from 2019, but now the pair are back with something a little easier to wear.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’.

Social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette. The toebox is white, the overlays are red, and the Swoosh and collar are black. But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

It has been revealed that the significant switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’.

It has been revealed that while you might normally expect this sort of massive Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

The Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

A version of this story originally appeared on British GQ.

Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta.
  • Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.
  • More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

It has been revealed that cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Recent findings suggest that add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Industry observers note that the winter season is just around the corner, which means the time to stock up on warm outerwear options is now. The best shearling jackets and coats are the wardrobe solution to get through the snow storms, polar vortexes, and mind-numbingly cold temperatures we will certainly face. A puffer coat might seem like the most sensible choice in most of these scenarios, but shearling coats and jackets provide a little more polish to every look, while still offering the warmth necessary to tide us over until spring.

Shearling outerwear has long been a wardrobe essential. It’s sturdy, durable, and made to last forever in your coat closet. Their timeless reputation makes them the perfect investment piece, an crucial fact to consider when shopping for items that you can love and own for years, and perhaps pass down one day. You can find faux options, otherwise billed as fleece or teddy, that look and feel just as good as the real thing.

Think of these shearling pieces as the easy outfit elevators in your late-fall and winter wardrobe, with plenty of styling possibilities. You need not go further than the FW26 runways for a jolt of inspiration. In Paris, Alaïa teamed impeccably tailored leather options, outfitted with sweeping asymmetric hemlines and monochromatic-toned shearling at the collar, with sporty joggers and semi-sheer stilettos. In Upcoming York, Altuzarra went the downtown-cool route with its offerings, pairing oversized shearling-adorned aviator jackets with Fair Isle knits and an array of leather and suede trousers in neutral olive and cream tones. This, in all honesty, is how I’ve been styling my favorite shearling jackets and coats for years: Over equally sumputous textures that lean into their inherent cozy-cool design ethos.

My pick of all the affordable, stylish offerings I’ve sourced—from J.Crew, Ralph Lauren, Dunst, and more—for the season ahead.

Sources indicate that I continue to fall in love with Gap. Details like bold contrast stitching across the shoulder and back, and a cropped, boxy fit instantly elevate a vegan leather jacket into something worth investing in.

I’ve been (attempting) to swap black for brown this season, so this shearling-lined jacket felt appropriate to include. The shearling trim balances its voluminous profile, so it won’t overwhelm my shorter frame.

You really can’t beat the classics. Oversized and high-collared, Dunst’s faux suede jacket is a modern take on a must-have style. The chocolate brown trim gives it warmth—and just enough contrast.

Recent findings suggest that J.Crew’s collarless coat gets a wintery overhaul courtesy of all-over beige shearling. As a longtime fan of the bestselling style, the new version caught my eye for its clean-lined, yet still layerable fit.

Combining two winter trends at once—peplum and shearling—Zara’s take on the shearling jacket trend is equal parts ladylike and stylish. I love how it toys with the idea of what a shearling jacket should look like—and I like where it’s headed.

In a recent development, belted with the faintest peplum, I immediately gravitated towards this fluffy collared option from H&M. A great piece to style with more casual bottoms in need of a little toughening up.

In a recent development, some jackets on this list bring the drama. This is not one of them. It’s simple in the best way—I love the idea of styling it with a black turtleneck underneath, and a red scarf wrapped around my neck.

It has been revealed that I love when a classic style gets a subtle revamp—and here, Mango gets it right: The chunky cuffs and wide lapel on this shearling jacket make it feel especially of the moment. Plus, the contrasting shades of brown between the leather and the shearling add interest.

In a recent development, rue Sophie’s mastered one of winter’s coolest trends by crafting a collarless option. This one would look great no matter how you style it, but we especially love with winter whites for a tonal take.

In a recent development, come for the Tasman slippers, stay for the outerwear that’s just as plush. This moto jacket reinterprets the traditional silhouette, giving it a roomier, boxier fit that’s great for layering. Size down if you want something closer to the body.

Of course Zara’s mastered one of winter’s coolest trends by crafting a reversible option. This black one looks great no matter which side you show, so you essentially get two jackets for the price of one.

Sources indicate that I gasped when I saw this parka. Here, more is more is more—the exaggerated collar, the voluminous down, the softly wrapped silhouette. It’s a great use case of where the coat is the outfit.

The sleek, collarless design on this duffle makes it equal parts wearable and on-trend. I’d lean into its coziness with corduroys and a festive Fair Isle knit.

Sometimes, you just need to throw on a long coat and get out the door. This one from & Other Stories is the solution to looking stylish when you’re low on time… and outfit ideas.

Recent findings suggest that I go to Madewell for two things: Jeans and outerwear. This sherpa-collared bomber jacket proves why. With softly rounded shoulders, it’s a versatile find that I would style with dark-wash denim, a close-fitting turtleneck, and boots.

According to recent reports, here’s another one for the extroverts. Apparis’s cropped jacket gives your typical shearling style a cool-girl upgrade with a faux leather trim; the hip-grazing length keeps it from going overboard. Style it with navy blue and black pieces to mix in other wearable neutrals.

Photographer Jessica Craig-Martin’s Upcoming Memoir Reveals the Life Behind Her “Drunken Lens”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor.
  • Since the early ’90s, photographer Jessica Craig-Martin has captured high society from unusual angles.
  • In a recent development, craig-Martin’s memoir, I Regret I Am Able to Attend, out now, tells the story of how she got there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Since the early ’90s, photographer Jessica Craig-Martin has captured high society from unusual angles. She zooms in on air kisses and other mannered gestures, cleavage in couture gowns, high heels, and the floors typically omitted from pristine event documentation, straddling the line between fashion photography and art portraiture.

In a recent development, craig-Martin’s memoir, I Regret I Am Able to Attend, out now, tells the story of how she got there. Craig-Martin details her bohemian childhood, wild friendships, and volatile young marriage with the effervescence that fills her compositions.

The story begins with the photographer’s parents, artists Michael Craig-Martin and Jan Hashey, who meet at the Yale School of Art. They have Jessica, then swiftly separate after revelations that they’re both having affairs, and Michael comes out as gay. From there, Craig-Martin experiences a peripatetic childhood, eventually settling in New York in her mother’s SoHo loft. Her creative milieu includes gallerist Paula Cooper and artists Elizabeth Murray, Jennifer Bartlett, and Joel Shapiro, along with their children. Craig-Martin gets a job at high-end grocer Dean & Deluca, where Basquiat comes in to buy smoked eel for a strange supper. Artists Brice and Helen Marden hire her to babysit their daughters, and soon she’s off to Morocco and Greece with the family.

Instead of attending college, Craig-Martin receives an alternative education as she lands a gig waitressing at Brian McNally’s celebrity-filled restaurant Indochine. She flies to London to start a job as a fashion assistant at Anna Wintour’s British Vogue (where they love her American enthusiasm), then back in New York, she works at Tina Brown’s Vanity Fair (where they love her British sophistication). Throughout the memoir, Craig-Martin captures the colorful characters who parade in and out of her life and around a rapidly evolving New York City.

Ahead of the book’s publication and her forthcoming show at the Andres Thalmann gallery in Paris, Bazaar spoke to Craig-Martin about her writing process and her shifting understanding of gender in the art world. We were on the telephone, and the artist was visiting “I Am Plane Image,” a show of Brice Marden’s paintings at Gagosian in Chelsea. A guard reprimanded her for getting too close to a painting. “When I was a kid, one was encouraged to touch the art,” she told me. “A lot of art was activated by the viewer. And now someone’s always saying, ‘Excuse me!’ ‘Excuse me!’ ”.

You’re a society photographer whose pictures conjure an entire milieu. Your book does something similar, but with language. How do you think about the relationship between writing and photography?

Sources indicate that it’s the same brain, making different things. With photography, I never thought about what I was going to make before I made it. I’d see something with my camera, and I’d have to grab it. It’s a wonderful feeling of adrenaline, and it’s similar to looking for the next word. Everything just disappears. There’s a loss of self in the process, and you become your purest self.

In the book, your aesthetic education seems to come, in part, from painter Brice Marden.

It has been revealed that with the camera, I felt a certain freedom. I really didn’t know much about photography, because it wasn’t a popular medium with my parents and their friends. And from Brice, I understood this freedom to put what you want in a picture. You can leave things out, push it around until it works, make it as weird as you want. If you feel like cutting off the top of a head in a photograph, try it!

In a recent development, I knew certain photographers, but not society photographers like Tina Barney and Larry Fink. I only knew a few pictures of Weegee’s. There was a lot for me to discover. If I’d seen more of this work, I would have felt inadequate. In this case, ignorance was bliss. Academic training can make you self-conscious. I didn’t have anything to unlearn.

Your mother has a philosophy that artists are the real aristocracy. Do you share it?

In a recent development, she was right about everything she stated. But it is extreme. I mean, we want doctors and we need other professions. But I think all artists believe this, as did all of us art brats who grew up in this kind of crazy, free-range situation. Art comes first. Everything else comes afterwards. It’s what we are in the truest form.

Industry observers note that good work rises to the top. Then again, not everyone whose work is good has been correctly honored or addressed. Women and people of color were left out of the discourse.

Your mother also says that Indochine is where you became a photographer.

I was raised in the very lean ’60s and ’70s, and then suddenly Fresh York just was drunk on money overnight. And this job threw me into the middle of it. It was a hot seat to view all this excess. I found my subject matter there. Everything’s moving at once, and I keep that feeling when I’m taking a photograph. There’s a lot of motion in my pictures, and I’m capturing the feet or I’m above the person or I’m not where a photographer would normally be. [Gallerist] Jeanne Greenberg calls it my “drunken lens.”.

The book is also a portrait of an evolving Fresh York. It’s more sanitized now.

Sources indicate that newly introduced York is still New York. We lose a lot with the corporatization of the city. But that’s global. It’s the same fuckers in every city making it into glass, concrete, steel with a bank in the bottom of the building and a Starbucks. It’s more painful here because New York is my city. But you can’t be too nostalgic because it’s also about speed and change. If you get stuck, you’re missing the point.

Recent findings suggest that the sex appeal is now in Brooklyn. I’m an old fart now, I don’t hang out, but I know there are young people who are opening galleries and making good art. It’s just harder and harder to find a crack in the sidewalk to grow out of.

Toward the end of the book, during your marriage to artist Ashley Bickerton, you write that you made “Art Wife Curry.” That comes shortly after your mention of Rirkrit Tiravanija making curry at 303 Gallery, which he just calls “art.” You write about the covert sexism in the art world versus the overt sexism in the restaurant world. In the writing process, did you come to think any differently about how gender had shaped you?

In a recent development, yeah. When you’re naive and you’re a young woman, you’re experiencing these invisible forces pushing you around, or men are behaving in a certain way, and you’re used to it. It’s like air. You don’t see it. And not just writing the book, but getting older, you can really see the forces that pulled you this way or that, where you felt a limitation. When I look back, I think, Why didn’t I just say “fuck you”? Or why didn’t I say, No, no, I’m coming through? Women second-guess themselves a great deal more than men. Men push and then afterwards say, Oh, did I break it? And then everyone claps. That’s not the classic woman’s story. There are corrections happening, and many of them are very well-deserved.

What kinds of limitations are you thinking about?

Sources indicate that it’s about confidence. Being an unquestioning force in the world and feeling like you have a right to be seen on the wall, have just as big a studio as your husband or partner. If you go to the Krasner Pollock home in Springs in Long Island, his studio was famously the barn, a giant empty space. And hers was this tiny room. That would be the normal order of things. That’s the way it was in my family, even though I thought of my parents as liberated. My mother was considered a star at Yale, and as soon as she left and had a baby, she was a mother first, artist second. My parents’ generation thought they had dealt with a lot of this second-classing of women, and they really hadn’t.

Sources indicate that the book ends when you’re around 35, your marriage is over, and your photography career has finally begun. Why end there? Will there be a Volume 2?

Good question. There might be. But I’ve also told my friends to tie me up and duct tape me to a wall if I ever start to try, because this was so difficult to make. I’m already forgetting how dreadful I found the experience.

#42964. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

In a recent development, cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

Joseph Zada of The Hunger Games Is Still Getting Used to Being a Movie Star

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark.
  • It has been revealed that his much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week.
  • According to recent reports, in the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark. And why shouldn’t he be?

It has been revealed that his much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his Fresh York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

According to recent reports, in the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”.

In a recent development, since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”.

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

According to recent reports, maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

No, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. The way they’ve set it up has just been otherworldly, and I’m not sure if I’ll ever have it again, but I distinctly remember each stop and the feelings that I’ve had thus far, and it doesn’t get old. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. So it’s a really special experience, and I don’t know when I’m going to be able to get that again.

It has been revealed that where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

Am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a big fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

You know I have some serious stompers.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

Industry observers note that I pride myself on my ability to have vulnerability. I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I modeled my career on people like Timothée Chalamet and Lucas Hedges, and I love the way that they kept their heart on their sleeve and how they feel like an open nerve. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

In a recent development, I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes and really, really felt like I was there every single day and just had the most incredible support in terms of my cast mates and my directors and my producers. And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

I guess everything just kind of changed just like that. Everything just changed in one quick second, and it feels like... I guess I haven’t really thought about what it was like before. I’ve just kind of been trying to ride the wave. I’m sure being able to go back home for Christmas, I’ll have some time to reflect, but right now it’s just—what’s the day ahead of me? And just making sure I’m ready for all of that.

Industry observers note that I’m just excited to be at home every single day and watch movies with my mom and my siblings and see all my friends. That’s what I’m really excited for. I’m just excited to also just turn off my phone for a little bit, maybe go on a little road trip down to South Australia and get a little beach house and not bring my phone and have six days where I’m just off the grid.

That’s a great question. I’ve got Apocalypse Now on 4K Ultra HD on my projector that I bought at home, and I cannot wait. I feel like people ask me what was the best part of my year, and I just start naming all the movies that I’ve watched. And genuinely the happiest that I ever am is when I’m watching a film, which is kind of sad but also kind of cool.

Industry observers note that I think... I don’t know. I loved Wild Horse Nine. That’s a favorite I’ve watched in cinemas. I loved Primetime too, because I love Rob Pattinson. I love Skyler Gisondo.

I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. It feels like every young male actor that I speak to feels like that is a person to look to right now and a person’s career to emulate in terms of the risks and the commitment to his craft and all these roles that he’s churning out.

I don’t know. It’s so ridiculously helpful to have a book with you because it’s just so much information, and I love preparing for roles and having a book because it’s just an internal monologue, which is what you should be doing for every character. You read a scene, and you should be writing what is going through your character’s head. And when you have a book, it’s all done for you, or at least you have a good foundation.

In a recent development, I hope I get to do as many book adaptations as possible, but I think what I’m really looking for is just a great director and a great script. I’m not sure what’s [next]. I’ve got a fresh slate right now, but there’s a couple of things floating around.

Latest Update: Totally Buggin'! Paid Nails Are Here for Fall

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Move over, fruit nails: this festive season, which means it’s time to go in a different direction with our nail designs.
  • In a recent development, the plaid nails trend can be more than just a vibe, though.
  • The preppy trend has long been permeating fashion, where there’s been no escaping the scholarly tropes of collegiate knit sweaters, check kilts, loafers, and classic trench coats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Move over, fruit nails: this festive season, which means it’s time to go in a different direction with our nail designs. The inspiration? Ralph Lauren Christmas, Linda Evangelista’s 1991 Scotland shoot, and obviously Cher’s iconic yellow suit. The trend is both warm and chic, seasonal and statement-making.

In a recent development, the plaid nails trend can be more than just a vibe, though. Try finding inspiration from heritage prints and textured knits—all the things you’ll be wearing in for the foreseeable. It’s sleek but striking, a combo of criss-crossed stripes in various lengths and widths. While you can go totally classic, plaid nails are also completely customizable, with lots of opportunity to get creative and add your own personal spin with the colors and line styles you or your nail tech paints on. Maybe your plaid nails come in that familiar curation of burgundy, cream, and navy blue, or you mix it up with lilacs and pinks.

The preppy trend has long been permeating fashion, where there’s been no escaping the scholarly tropes of collegiate knit sweaters, check kilts, loafers, and classic trench coats. Think Michael Rider’s cinched Argyle knits in his Resort collection for Celine, Ralph Lauren’s ever-enduring allegiance to check, and The Row’s own selection of knits. It was only a matter of time before the school of prep swept beauty too—be the best student in class, and match your next set to your polo and skirt.

Industry observers note that kylie Jenner looked to her go-to nail artist, Zola Ganzorigt, for her own striped manicure. Ganzorigt—who is always first on the trends or coining them herself, a la Hailey Bieber’s glazed donut nails—opted for a colorful selection of colors to create the look, with each long, almond-shaped plaid nail in a different combo: One chocolate and butter yellow, one lilac and moss green, one inky blue and gray.

Baltimore-based nail artist @nailology.101’s plaid nails take a more cool-toned approach, with a silvery base and gradient stripes in forest green, icy blue, and red—they look expensive.

Sarah Brezel demonstrated off a colorful but classic palette, pairing plum and lilac, moss green and navy, deep cherry red and burnt orange.

Sources indicate that dress up a classic French mani with plaid print, like this fabulous set. Nail artist Pitrizz Gangcuangco says this was a more muted take, mixing a bold yellow plaid pattern on top of a neutral base. Gangcuangco calls the teddy bear charm a fun and cozy touch.

It has been revealed that A cool-toned brown shade is the perfect staple for fall. Add in plaid details, like celebrity and Chanel nail artist Betina Goldstein did here, to make them feel a bit more seasonal and cozy. The white, black, and blue lines are the perfect combo that really pop against the chocolate shade.

Sources indicate that plaid inspo can come from anywhere. For this pink shimmer plaid look, nail artist Shannon Elias took inspiration from her client’s matching custom-made dress. To get that cat-eye shimmer, she used a magnet to add some depth. “I love how this set turned out and will never get tired of this pattern,” she says. “I’m already looking forward to recreating more coming into this festive season.”.

As major proponents of mixing different designs, this combo of argyle prints and cat-eye finishes just speaks to us. Celebrity nail artist Queenie Nguyen uses deep blues and greens to really make the a bold statement with the plaid. And it’s just super fun.

This smooth, velvet finish is just so dreamy. Nail artist San Sung Kim says she was inspired by her favorite plaid sweater and opted for bright colors that still felt cozy. To get that velvet finish, she used a magnet for extra shine and glitter.

Recent findings suggest that so how will you be styling your own plaid nails for fall? Whatever your aesthetic, if you’re embracing prep, be sure to prep your nails accordingly with a good shaping, cuticle tidy, and strengthening base coat. Start with a neutral base polish to make your design pop like a true plaid, and keep a super steady hand for that intricate striping. Go forth, prepsters!

How can someone create a plaid nail look at home?

Recent findings suggest that “Anyone can create a plaid look with just a few velvet polishes or jelly polishes,” says Kim. She says you just need to paint on a few stripes of one color in one direction, followed by a different color in the same direction. Then finish by painting on different sizes of stripes and colors in another direction for added dimension.
